title: BlackByte
summary: BlackByte is a ransomware operation, also tracked as Hecamede, that has been active in public reporting since around 2021. It follows the double extortion model: affiliates steal data first, then encrypt it, and publish victim names on a leak site to pressure payment. Public reporting describes an affiliate model, so different intrusions use different entry paths, including phishing and the exploitation of internet facing services that were not patched. Typical intrusions use commodity tooling such as Cobalt Strike beacons and commercial remote monitoring software for hands on keyboard work, plus credential dumping, before a dedicated encryptor runs. Evidence sits in Windows event logs, remote access tool artifacts, command line arguments, backup deletion records and a ransom note dropped on disk. Attribution of the individuals behind the brand is contested and rests mainly on shared tooling and infrastructure overlap rather than direct proof.

beginner.definition: BlackByte is a group of criminals who use ransomware, which is software that locks files and asks for money to unlock them. Security researchers also call this group Hecamede. It is not a single computer program; it is a team that breaks into networks and then demands payment.
beginner.whyItMatters: If this group enters your network, your files can be locked and your private data can be stolen. They copy the data first, then they lock the files. This means paying the ransom does not promise that your secrets stay private. Many small companies never fully recover, and some close for good. Knowing the warning signs helps you react in the first hours, when it still matters.
howItWorks: They get in through a stolen password or an old program with a known hole.
They use normal remote support tools so their activity looks like a real employee.
They collect more passwords and move from one computer to the next.
They copy important files out of the network before they lock anything.
They delete the backup copies, so recovery becomes much harder.
They run their locker program and leave a note that demands payment.
beginner.example: Picture a warehouse with one shared key. A thief copies the key at night, makes a copy of every list of goods, then changes the locks and leaves a note on the door. The owner now has two problems. The stock is locked inside, and the thief already knows exactly what was in there. Backups kept in a different building, under a different lock, are what save the business. Paying the thief is like trusting a stranger to send the new key later.
takeaways: They steal data first, so paying does not keep your secrets private.
Keep backups offline, because they often delete the online copies.
Unusual remote access tool use is an early warning sign, so watch for it.

objectives: Explain what double extortion ransomware is and why paying does not remove the data theft risk.
Describe the affiliate model and why two BlackByte intrusions can look completely different.
Identify the log and tool artifacts that reveal remote access tool abuse on a Windows host.
Summarise the value of offline, tested backups during a ransomware recovery.
Discuss why public attribution of a ransomware brand is usually held with low confidence.
